title: Dividing with a Remainder
description: What the lemma says and why the remainder is always smaller than the divisor.

blocks.heading: The idea
blocks.body: Divide 17 by 5: you get 3 groups of 5 and 2 left over. So 17 = 5 x 3 + 2. The leftover is always less than 5, otherwise you could make another group.

blocks.heading: The lemma
blocks.body: a = bq + r, where 0 <= r < b

blocks.heading: Remember
blocks.body:
q and r are unique
r can be 0
b must be positive

blocks.heading: Try it
blocks.body: Write 58 in the form 7q + r. 58 = 7 x 8 + 2, so q = 8, r = 2.

title: Euclid's Algorithm for HCF
description: Repeat the lemma until the remainder is zero to find the HCF fast.

blocks.heading: Why it works
blocks.body: Any common factor of a and b also divides r = a - bq. So HCF(a, b) = HCF(b, r), and the pair keeps getting smaller.

blocks.heading: Worked example
blocks.body: HCF(196, 38220): 38220 = 196 x 195 + 0. Remainder is already 0, so HCF = 196.

blocks.heading: Checklist
blocks.body:
Larger number first
Stop at remainder 0
Answer is the last divisor, not the last quotient

title: Prime Factorisation
description: Break numbers into primes using a factor tree and see why the result is unique.

blocks.heading: Building blocks
blocks.body: Primes are the atoms of numbers. 360 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 x 5 = 2^3 x 3^2 x 5, and no other list of primes multiplies to 360.

blocks.heading: Method
blocks.body:
Divide by the smallest prime repeatedly
Move to the next prime when it stops dividing
Write the answer with exponents

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: Factorise 1001: 1001 = 7 x 11 x 13.

title: HCF and LCM from Primes
description: Use prime factorisations to get HCF and LCM and check with the product rule.

blocks.heading: Rules
blocks.body:
HCF: smallest power of each common prime
LCM: largest power of every prime present
HCF x LCM = a x b

blocks.heading: Why 3^n never ends in 0
blocks.body: A number ending in 0 needs both 2 and 5 as prime factors. 3^n has only 3s, so it never ends in 0.

blocks.heading: Traps
blocks.body:
HCF uses the smallest powers
The product rule is for two numbers only

title: Zeros of a Polynomial
description: What a zero means algebraically and on the graph.

blocks.heading: Definition
blocks.body: k is a zero of p(x) if p(k) = 0. For p(x) = x^2 - 4, both 2 and -2 are zeros because they make p(x) zero.

blocks.heading: On the graph
blocks.body: The curve of a quadratic is a parabola. Its zeros are where it cuts the x-axis. It can cut twice, touch once, or never meet the axis.

blocks.heading: Check
blocks.body: Is 3 a zero of x^2 - 2x - 3? p(3) = 9 - 6 - 3 = 0. Yes.

title: Sum and Product of Zeros
description: The relations between zeros and coefficients, and how to build a polynomial from its zeros.

blocks.heading: Relations
blocks.body: For ax^2 + bx + c: alpha + beta = -b/a and alpha x beta = c/a

blocks.heading: Verify
blocks.body: 3x^2 - 12x + 9: zeros 1 and 3. Sum 4 = 12/3, product 3 = 9/3.

blocks.heading: Build
blocks.body: Zeros 2 and -5: sum -3, product -10. Polynomial x^2 + 3x - 10.

blocks.heading: Watch out
blocks.body:
The minus sign in -b/a
a is the coefficient of x^2, not of x

title: Recognising a Quadratic
description: Rearrange any equation into ax^2 + bx + c = 0 and read the coefficients.

blocks.heading: Standard form
blocks.body: A quadratic equation has degree 2 once simplified. Expand brackets, move everything to one side, and combine like terms before deciding.

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: (x - 2)(x + 1) = x^2 - 3 becomes x^2 - x - 2 = x^2 - 3, so -x + 1 = 0. The square terms cancel: not a quadratic.

blocks.heading: Rule
blocks.body:
a is never 0 in a quadratic
Read b and c only from the standard form

title: Forming Quadratics from Word Problems
description: Turn a story into an equation by choosing the unknown well.

blocks.heading: Method
blocks.body: Let the unknown be the quantity asked for. Translate each sentence into an expression. Set up the equality the problem describes. Rearrange to standard form.

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: The product of two consecutive positive integers is 306. Let the smaller be x: x(x + 1) = 306, so x^2 + x - 306 = 0.

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: A train covers 480 km at speed x km/h. If it were 8 km/h slower it would take 3 h more: 480/(x - 8) - 480/x = 3, which simplifies to x^2 - 8x - 1280 = 0.

title: Splitting the Middle Term
description: The core factorisation technique, step by step.

blocks.heading: The technique
blocks.body: For ax^2 + bx + c, find two numbers whose product is a x c and whose sum is b. Rewrite bx as the sum of those two terms, then factor by grouping.

blocks.heading: Example with a = 1
blocks.body: x^2 + 5x + 6: product 6, sum 5 gives 2 and 3. (x + 2)(x + 3) = 0, so x = -2 or -3.

blocks.heading: Signs
blocks.body:
Product positive, sum positive: both positive
Product positive, sum negative: both negative
Product negative: one of each, larger magnitude takes the sign of b

title: The Quadratic Formula
description: Solve any quadratic with the formula and know when to reach for it.

blocks.heading: Formula
blocks.body: x = [-b +/- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)] / 2a

blocks.heading: When to use it
blocks.body: Use the formula when the middle term will not split neatly, or when the roots are irrational. It always works when b^2 - 4ac >= 0.

blocks.heading: Common slips
blocks.body:
Write -b, then square b separately
Divide the whole numerator by 2a
Simplify the square root before dividing

title: Word Problems and Checking Roots
description: Set up, solve, then reject roots that make no sense.

blocks.heading: Reject impossible roots
blocks.body: Lengths, ages, counts and speeds cannot be negative or fractional when the story says they are whole. Always check both roots against the situation.

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: A rectangle has area 60 and its length is 7 more than its breadth. b(b + 7) = 60 gives b^2 + 7b - 60 = 0, (b + 12)(b - 5) = 0. b = -12 is rejected; breadth 5, length 12.

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: Two numbers differ by 3 and their product is 54: x(x + 3) = 54, x^2 + 3x - 54 = 0, (x + 9)(x - 6) = 0, so 6 and 9, or -9 and -6 if negatives are allowed.

blocks.heading: Always
blocks.body:
Substitute each root back into the original equation
Answer the question asked, not just x

title: The Discriminant
description: Predict the type of roots without solving.

blocks.heading: Discriminant
blocks.body: D = b^2 - 4ac

blocks.heading: Three cases
blocks.body:
D > 0: two distinct real roots
D = 0: two equal real roots
D < 0: no real roots

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: x^2 + x + 1 = 0: D = 1 - 4 = -3, no real roots.

title: Finding Unknown Coefficients
description: Use D = 0 to find a parameter that gives equal roots.

blocks.heading: Method
blocks.body: Write D in terms of the unknown, set it equal to 0, solve the resulting equation. Check that a is still non-zero.

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: 2x^2 + kx + 3 = 0 has equal roots: k^2 - 24 = 0, so k = +/- 2 sqrt 6.

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: kx(x - 2) + 6 = 0 has equal roots: kx^2 - 2kx + 6 = 0, D = 4k^2 - 24k = 0, so k = 6 (k = 0 rejected).

title: Velocity and Time
description: The first equation of motion and the meaning of acceleration.

blocks.heading: Acceleration
blocks.body: Acceleration is the change in velocity per second. If a car goes from 10 m/s to 20 m/s in 5 s, its velocity changed by 10 m/s over 5 s, so a = 2 m/s^2.

blocks.heading: First equation
blocks.body: v = u + at

blocks.heading: Units
blocks.body:
Velocity in m/s
Acceleration in m/s^2
Time in s
Convert km/h by multiplying by 5/18

title: Displacement Equations
description: The second and third equations and how to choose between them.

blocks.heading: Choosing
blocks.body: List what you know and what you want. If time is not involved, use v^2 = u^2 + 2as. If final velocity is not involved, use s = ut + (1/2)at^2.

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: A ball dropped from rest falls for 3 s (a = 10 m/s^2): s = 0 + 0.5 x 10 x 9 = 45 m.

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: A bike at 15 m/s brakes at -3 m/s^2 to rest: 0 = 225 + 2(-3)s, so s = 37.5 m.

blocks.heading: Signs
blocks.body:
Choose the direction of motion as positive
Retardation gives negative a

title: Writing and Balancing Equations
description: From word equation to balanced symbol equation with states.

blocks.heading: Why balance
blocks.body: Atoms rearrange in a reaction but none appear or vanish. A balanced equation shows this with equal atom counts on both sides.

blocks.heading: Steps
blocks.body:
Write correct formulas
Count atoms of each element
Adjust coefficients, starting with the element in the fewest formulas
Balance H and O last
Recheck everything

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: Zn + HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2. Cl: 1 vs 2, so 2HCl. Now H: 2 vs 2. Balanced: Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2.

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: C3H8 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O. C: 3CO2. H: 4H2O. O on right: 6 + 4 = 10, so 5O2. Balanced: C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O.

title: Types of Reactions
description: Combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement and redox with everyday examples.

blocks.heading: Combination and decomposition
blocks.body: Combination: two substances form one (CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2). Decomposition: one breaks into several, often by heat, light or electricity (2H2O -> 2H2 + O2 by electrolysis).

blocks.heading: Displacement
blocks.body: A more reactive element pushes out a less reactive one: Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu. The blue solution turns green.

blocks.heading: Double displacement and redox
blocks.body: Ions swap partners: Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 + 2NaCl (white precipitate). In redox one substance gains oxygen (oxidised) while another loses it (reduced).

blocks.heading: Spotting them
blocks.body:
Two in, one out: combination
One in, many out: decomposition
Element swaps with element: displacement
Ions swap: double displacement

title: Two ways to measure a journey
description: Why physics needs both distance and displacement.

blocks.heading: The idea
blocks.body: Imagine walking to a shop 200 m away and back home. You covered 400 m of path, yet you are exactly where you started. Physics keeps both facts: the path length is distance, the start-to-end change is displacement.

blocks.heading: Remember
blocks.body:
Distance: scalar, never negative
Displacement: vector, needs a direction
Equal only for one-way straight-line motion

blocks.heading: Try it
blocks.body: Walk 6 m north then 8 m east. Distance is 14 m. Displacement is sqrt(36 + 64) = 10 m, north-east.

blocks.heading: Rule
blocks.body: |displacement| <= distance

title: Rates of change
description: From speed to velocity to acceleration in one chain.

blocks.heading: Speed and velocity
blocks.body: Both tell you how fast. Speed uses distance, velocity uses displacement, so velocity also tells you which way. A car going round a roundabout at a steady 20 km/h has constant speed but changing velocity.

blocks.heading: Acceleration
blocks.body: a = (v - u) / t

blocks.heading: Signs
blocks.body:
Choose a positive direction first
Velocity opposite to it is negative
Acceleration against the velocity slows the object

blocks.heading: Worked
blocks.body: A train goes from 72 km/h (20 m/s) to rest in 40 s. a = (0 - 20)/40 = -0.5 m/s^2. The minus sign means retardation.

title: Reading motion from a graph
description: What slopes and areas mean on each kind of graph.

blocks.heading: Distance-time graphs
blocks.body: Time runs along the bottom, distance up the side. A steeper line means more distance in the same time, so a higher speed. A flat line means the object is not moving.

blocks.heading: Velocity-time graphs
blocks.body: Now velocity is up the side. A flat line is constant velocity. A rising straight line is constant acceleration. The area between the line and the time axis is how far the object went.

blocks.heading: Two slopes, one area
blocks.body:
Slope of d-t = speed
Slope of v-t = acceleration
Area under v-t = displacement

blocks.heading: Worked
blocks.body: Velocity rises from 0 to 20 m/s in 5 s then stays there for 5 s. Displacement = triangle (0.5 x 5 x 20 = 50 m) + rectangle (5 x 20 = 100 m) = 150 m.

title: Force, inertia and momentum
description: The three laws with the questions each one answers.

blocks.heading: First law
blocks.body: Without a net force, nothing changes: rest stays rest, motion stays uniform. That resistance to change is inertia, and mass measures it. A frame where the first law holds is an inertial frame.

blocks.heading: Second law
blocks.body: F_net = dp/dt = ma (constant mass)

blocks.heading: Third law
blocks.body: Forces are interactions. When the ground pushes you forward, you push the ground backward with exactly the same force. The pair acts on two different bodies, which is why they can never cancel each other.

blocks.heading: Free-body diagrams
blocks.body:
Draw one body at a time
Include every force on that body only
Resolve along and perpendicular to motion
Apply F_net = ma along each axis

blocks.heading: Worked
blocks.body: A 3 kg block on a frictionless table is pulled by 12 N. a = 12/3 = 4 m/s^2. Add 3 N friction: a = (12 - 3)/3 = 3 m/s^2.

title: The self-adjusting force
description: Static, limiting and kinetic friction, and the normal force behind them.

blocks.heading: Static friction
blocks.body: Push a heavy box gently and it does not move: friction matches your push exactly. Push harder and friction rises with you, up to a limit. Beyond that the box slides and kinetic friction takes over.

blocks.heading: Limits
blocks.body: f_s <= mu_s N and f_k = mu_k N, with mu_k < mu_s

blocks.heading: Normal force
blocks.body:
Level ground: N = mg
Incline: N = mg cos(theta)
Extra downward push increases N and hence friction

blocks.heading: Angle of repose
blocks.body: A block just begins to slide when the incline reaches theta with tan(theta) = mu_s. For mu_s = 0.58, theta is about 30 degrees.

title: Why turning needs a force
description: Centripetal acceleration and who provides it.

blocks.heading: Turning is accelerating
blocks.body: Speed may be steady, but the direction of velocity changes every instant. That change is an acceleration of size v^2/r pointing to the centre of the circle.

blocks.heading: Centripetal force
blocks.body: F_c = mv^2 / r

blocks.heading: Who supplies it
blocks.body:
Stone on a string: tension
Car on a level road: friction
Satellite: gravity
Banked road: part of the normal force

blocks.heading: Level road
blocks.body: With mu = 0.4 and r = 40 m, v_max = sqrt(0.4 x 40 x 10) = 12.6 m/s, about 45 km/h. Faster and the car skids outward.

title: Five kinds of change
description: How to name a reaction by looking at what it does.

blocks.heading: Look at the shape
blocks.body: Count how many substances go in and come out. One product from many: combination. Many from one: decomposition. An element swapping into a compound: displacement. Two compounds trading partners: double displacement.

blocks.heading: Energy
blocks.body:
Exothermic releases heat: burning, quicklime in water
Endothermic absorbs heat: most decompositions
Photolytic decomposition uses light: AgBr in photography

blocks.heading: Worked
blocks.body: Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu. Iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces it. The blue solution turns green and copper deposits on the nail.

blocks.heading: Precipitation
blocks.body: Na2SO4(aq) + BaCl2(aq) -> BaSO4(s) + 2NaCl(aq)

title: Redox in the kitchen and on the bridge
description: Oxidation, reduction, rust and rancid oil.

blocks.heading: Two halves of one change
blocks.body: When copper oxide is heated in hydrogen, oxygen moves from copper to hydrogen. Copper oxide is reduced, hydrogen is oxidised. The giver of oxygen is the oxidising agent.

blocks.heading: Agents
blocks.body:
Oxidising agent: gets reduced
Reducing agent: gets oxidised
Redox = both together

blocks.heading: Rust
blocks.body: An iron nail in a dry test tube stays bright; in boiled water under oil it stays bright; in ordinary water with air it rusts. Both air and moisture are needed.

blocks.heading: Rust
blocks.body: 4Fe + 3O2 + xH2O -> 2Fe2O3.xH2O

title: Counting by weighing
description: Why chemists use the mole and how to convert with it.

blocks.heading: The chemist's dozen
blocks.body: Atoms are too small to count, so we weigh them. A mole of anything is 6.022 x 10^23 particles, and the molar mass tells you how many grams that is. Carbon: 12 g per mole. Water: 18 g per mole.

blocks.heading: Conversions
blocks.body: n = m/M    N = n x 6.022 x 10^23    V(gas, STP) = 22.4 n L

blocks.heading: Molar mass
blocks.body:
Add atomic masses using subscripts
H2SO4 = 2 + 32 + 64 = 98 g/mol
Diatomic gases: O2 = 32, N2 = 28, Cl2 = 71

blocks.heading: Worked
blocks.body: How many molecules are in 9 g of water? n = 9/18 = 0.5 mol. N = 0.5 x 6.022 x 10^23 = 3.011 x 10^23 molecules.

title: Recipes for molecules
description: Using mole ratios, spotting the limiting reagent, finding formulas.

blocks.heading: Ratios, not grams
blocks.body: A balanced equation is a recipe in moles. 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O says two moles of hydrogen need one mole of oxygen. Always convert grams to moles before using the recipe.

blocks.heading: Limiting reagent in three steps
blocks.body:
Convert each reactant to moles
Divide by its coefficient
The smallest result is the limiting reagent

blocks.heading: Worked
blocks.body: 10 g of Mg (0.417 mol) with 10 g of O2 (0.3125 mol) in 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. Divide by coefficients: Mg 0.208, O2 0.3125. Mg limits; MgO formed = 0.417 mol = 16.7 g.

blocks.heading: Formulas
blocks.body: Empirical: simplest ratio.   Molecular = (M / empirical mass) x empirical

title: How strong is the solution?
description: Molarity, molality, mole fraction and dilution.

blocks.heading: Three yardsticks
blocks.body: Molarity measures against the volume of the whole solution, molality against the mass of solvent, and mole fraction against total moles. Choose molality when temperature changes, because volume expands but mass does not.

blocks.heading: Definitions
blocks.body: M = n / V(L)    m = n / w_solvent(kg)    x_A = n_A / n_total

blocks.heading: Watch the units
blocks.body:
Convert mL to L for molarity
Convert g of solvent to kg for molality
Mole fractions of all components add to 1

blocks.heading: Dilution
blocks.body: How much water to add to 100 mL of 2 M HCl to get 0.5 M? M1V1 = M2V2: 2 x 100 = 0.5 x V2, V2 = 400 mL, so add 300 mL.

title: From story to equation
description: A four-step method for quadratic word problems.

blocks.heading: Four steps
blocks.body:
Name the unknown
Write the relation from the story
Bring to ax^2 + bx + c = 0 and solve
Reject roots that make no sense

blocks.heading: Speed
blocks.body: A train covers 360 km at speed x km/h. If the speed were 5 km/h more it would take 1 h less: 360/x - 360/(x + 5) = 1 -> x^2 + 5x - 1800 = 0 -> (x + 45)(x - 40) = 0 -> x = 40 km/h.

blocks.heading: Age
blocks.body: A father's age is x^2 where x is his son's age; in 9 years the father will be three times as old: x^2 + 9 = 3(x + 9) -> x^2 - 3x - 18 = 0 -> x = 6. Son 6, father 36.

blocks.heading: Checking
blocks.body: The other root, -3, is meaningless for an age. Always write one line saying why you rejected it.

title: A new kind of number
description: What i is and how to calculate with it.

blocks.heading: Why i
blocks.body: x^2 + 1 = 0 has no real solution. Define i with i^2 = -1 and it has two: i and -i. Every complex number is a real part plus i times another real part.

blocks.heading: Powers of i
blocks.body: i, -1, -i, 1, i, -1, ... repeating every four

blocks.heading: Arithmetic
blocks.body:
Add: (a + ib) + (c + id) = (a + c) + i(b + d)
Multiply like brackets, then replace i^2 with -1
Divide: multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the bottom

title: Picturing complex numbers
description: Points, distances and angles in the Argand plane.

blocks.heading: Points in a plane
blocks.body: Real numbers live on a line. Complex numbers need a plane: real part across, imaginary part up. 3 + 4i is the point (3, 4), five units from the origin.

blocks.heading: Modulus and argument
blocks.body: |z| = sqrt(a^2 + b^2),  tan(arg z) = b/a (fix the quadrant)

blocks.heading: Quadrants
blocks.body:
a > 0, b > 0: t = arctan(b/a)
a < 0, b > 0: t = pi - arctan(|b/a|)
a < 0, b < 0: t = -pi + arctan(|b/a|)
a > 0, b < 0: t = -arctan(|b/a|)

blocks.heading: Worked
blocks.body: z = -1 - i. r = sqrt(2). Third quadrant: t = -3pi/4. z = sqrt(2)(cos(-3pi/4) + i sin(-3pi/4)).

title: No real roots is not no roots
description: Extending the quadratic formula into the complex plane.

blocks.heading: The formula still works
blocks.body: When b^2 - 4ac is negative, its square root is i times the square root of the positive number. Nothing else changes.

blocks.heading: Roots
blocks.body: x = [-b +/- i sqrt(4ac - b^2)] / 2a

blocks.heading: Pairs
blocks.body:
Real coefficients give conjugate roots
Sum = -b/a, product = c/a still hold
Check by substituting back

title: Seeing the unit of life
description: How the microscope revealed cells and what the cell theory says.

blocks.heading: Cork and a microscope
blocks.body: In 1665 Robert Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork under his microscope and saw tiny boxes. He called them cells. Later Leeuwenhoek saw living cells swimming in pond water.

blocks.heading: Cell theory
blocks.body:
All organisms are made of cells
The cell is the basic unit of structure and function
New cells arise from pre-existing cells (Virchow)

blocks.heading: Variety
blocks.body: A hen's egg is a single cell you can see. A nerve cell can be a metre long. A red blood cell has no nucleus so it can carry more haemoglobin.

title: The cell's gatekeeper
description: How the plasma membrane lets things in and out.

blocks.heading: Selective
blocks.body: The membrane is not a wall. Gases slip through by diffusion, water crosses by osmosis, and larger molecules are moved with the cell's help. This selectivity keeps the inside different from the outside.

blocks.heading: Three solutions
blocks.body:
Hypotonic outside: water in, cell swells
Isotonic: balance, no change
Hypertonic outside: water out, cell shrinks

blocks.heading: Egg experiment
blocks.body: A de-shelled egg in water swells; the same egg in concentrated salt solution shrinks. Only the water moves through the membrane.

blocks.heading: Plasmolysis
blocks.body: Put Rhoeo leaf cells in strong salt solution and the contents pull away from the cell wall. Return them to water and they recover.

title: A tour inside the cell
description: What each organelle does and how plant and animal cells differ.

blocks.heading: Control and building
blocks.body:
Nucleus: instructions in DNA
Rough ER: proteins
Smooth ER: lipids, detoxification
Golgi: packaging and delivery

blocks.heading: Energy, digestion, storage
blocks.body:
Mitochondria: ATP, the powerhouse
Lysosomes: digestion, suicide bags
Plastids: chloroplasts, chromoplasts, leucoplasts
Vacuoles: storage, turgor in plants

blocks.heading: Plant vs animal
blocks.body: Plant cells: cell wall of cellulose, chloroplasts, one large central vacuole. Animal cells: no wall, no chloroplasts, small vacuoles, centrioles.

blocks.heading: Self-sufficient organelles
blocks.body: Mitochondria and plastids carry their own DNA and ribosomes, so they can make some of their own proteins.

title: Two kinds of cells
description: What separates bacteria from the cells of plants and animals.

blocks.heading: Prokaryote
blocks.body: The genetic material is a naked circular DNA lying in the cytoplasm, the nucleoid. There is a cell wall outside the membrane and often a slimy glycocalyx outside that. Ribosomes are 70S. Some bacteria fold their membrane inward into mesosomes.

blocks.heading: Eukaryote
blocks.body: DNA is wrapped with proteins into chromosomes inside a nucleus with a double membrane. Membrane-bound organelles divide the labour, ribosomes are 80S, and a protein cytoskeleton gives shape and movement.

blocks.heading: Bacterial extras
blocks.body:
Plasmids: small circular DNA
Flagella with basal body, hook, filament
Pili and fimbriae for attachment
Gram positive vs Gram negative walls

blocks.heading: Endosymbiosis hint
blocks.body: Mitochondria and chloroplasts have 70S ribosomes and circular DNA, like bacteria, suggesting they were once free-living prokaryotes.

title: Boundaries and the shipping system
description: Membrane model, wall layers and the ER-Golgi pathway.

blocks.heading: Fluid mosaic
blocks.body: Singer and Nicolson pictured the membrane as a sea of phospholipids with protein icebergs. Lipids and proteins can drift sideways, which lets the membrane grow, pinch off vesicles and heal.

blocks.heading: Transport
blocks.body:
Simple diffusion: down the gradient, no energy
Osmosis: water across a semipermeable membrane
Active transport: against the gradient, uses ATP, e.g. sodium-potassium pump

blocks.heading: Endomembrane system
blocks.body:
Rough ER makes proteins and sends them on
Golgi modifies, sorts, packages
Lysosomes digest
Vacuoles store

blocks.heading: Plant wall
blocks.body: Middle lamella (calcium pectate) between neighbours, primary wall that stretches as the cell grows, secondary wall added inside for strength. Plasmodesmata are channels through the wall.

title: The control centre and the scaffolding
description: Nucleus, chromosome types and organelles without membranes.

blocks.heading: Nucleus
blocks.body: A double membrane with pores lets RNA out and proteins in. Inside, the nucleolus manufactures ribosomal RNA, and chromatin holds the DNA wound around histone proteins. During division chromatin packs into visible chromosomes.

blocks.heading: Chromosome types
blocks.body:
Metacentric: centromere in the middle
Submetacentric: slightly away from the middle
Acrocentric: close to one end
Telocentric: at the very end

blocks.heading: Without membranes
blocks.body:
Ribosomes: protein factories, 80S in eukaryotes
Cytoskeleton: microtubules, microfilaments, intermediate filaments
Cilia and flagella: 9 + 2 axoneme
Centrioles: 9 triplets, organise spindle

blocks.heading: Satellite
blocks.body: Some chromosomes have a secondary constriction that marks off a small satellite; these regions are nucleolar organisers.
